This is absolutely a problem we have today. Processors aren't getting faster. They're getting wider. Individual chips aren't getting faster, they're putting more chips on the die. But nobody has successfully figured out a way to make a single application fully utilize multiple cores. You can only spin off so many background processes. The main branch of applications still has be mostly synchronous. Let's look at the simple task of a contact form on a website.

  • Validate the from address
  • Validate the to address
  • Ensure the subject is not blank
  • Ensure the message is not blank
  • Establish a connection to the mail server
  • Stream the message
  • Wait for an acknowledgement from the mail server
  • Report back to the user that the message has been sent

Steps 1 - 4 can be spun off into background processes. Each step can be done by a different CPU. But steps 5 through 8 can't be spun off. They have to take place one after another. You can't do step 6 until step 5 has completed. The steps that you have spun off are insignificant. They are 50% of the steps, but only account for 10% of the processing power. In fact in this example the act of spinning off those steps is actually more expensive than doing it on a single core because there is still an overhead for spinning off a process.

That's the challenge for operating system designers today.
